## The three chains

```rust
fn evens_squared_sum(xs: &[i64]) -> i64 {
    xs.iter().filter(|x| *x % 2 == 0).map(|x| x * x).sum()
}

fn longest(words: &[String]) -> Option<&String> {
    words.iter().max_by_key(|w| w.len())
}

fn running(xs: &[i64]) -> Vec<i64> {
    xs.iter().scan(0i64, |acc, x| { *acc += x; Some(*acc) }).collect()
}
```

Each is one expression, and each is doing something a loop would need
three or four lines and a mutable variable for.

## The references, and why there are so many

`xs.iter()` yields `&i64`, not `i64`, because the slice is borrowed and
the iterator does not own anything. Then:

- `map(|x| x * x)` works directly, because `&i64 * &i64` is implemented.
- `filter(|x| ...)` hands the closure a **reference to the item** — so
  `x` is `&&i64` and the condition needs a dereference. `*x % 2 == 0`
  works; so does destructuring in the pattern, `filter(|&&x| x % 2 == 0)`.

That extra layer is not Rust being awkward. `filter` must not consume
the item it is deciding about, so it can only lend it, and the item is
already a reference. Writing `.copied()` after `.iter()` makes it go
away at the cost of a copy per element, which for `i64` is free.

## `sum()` and the type it sums into

`sum()` is generic over what it produces, so on its own it is ambiguous.
Here the return type of the function pins it to `i64`. Elsewhere you
will need `sum::<i64>()` or a typed binding, and "type annotations
needed" is the error that says so.

## Ties, and reading the documentation

`max_by_key` returns the **last** maximum when several compare equal;
`min_by_key` returns the first. That asymmetry is deliberate and
documented, and this exercise specifies the same behaviour so that the
obvious chain is the correct one. The hidden case with two equally long
words checks it, because "whichever one it happens to return" is not a
specification.

## `scan` against `fold`

`fold` carries an accumulator and produces one value at the end.
`scan` carries an accumulator and produces one value at **every** step,
which is exactly a running total.

The closure returns `Option`, and that is not decoration: returning
`None` ends the iteration there. That makes `scan` usable as a
take-while with state — "keep going until the total exceeds 100" is a
one-liner — and it means a `scan` that forgets to wrap its result in
`Some` does not compile rather than silently stopping.

## Why chains rather than loops

The chain says what is being computed; a loop says how. Beyond
readability there are two practical gains:

- **The compiler sees more.** These adaptors are zero-cost: the iterator
  chain compiles to the same machine code as a hand-written loop, and
  usually to a better one, because the bounds checks are provably
  unnecessary.
- **There is no accumulator to get wrong.** A `mut total` declared
  outside a loop is a variable that can be read before it is finished,
  reset in the wrong place, or shared with the next loop by accident.
  `scan`'s accumulator cannot escape the chain.
